questions.question: A, B, and C run a 1200 m race. A gives to B a headstart of 300 m, and to C a headstart of 600 m. A finishes the race 30 seconds before B and 60 seconds before C. If A’s speed is 10 m/s, then find the respective speeds of B and C. [Give your answer in m/s, and round off, wherever necessary, to one place after decimal.]
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__ 

A runs 1200 m at 10 m/s ⇒ time = 120 s

B runs 900 m and finishes 30 s later ⇒ time = 150 s

Speed of B = 900 / 150 = 6 m/s

C runs 600 m and finishes 60 s later ⇒ time = 180 s

Speed of C = 600 / 180 = 3.3 m/s

**∴ Answer: B = 6 m/s, C = 3.3 m/s**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__** 

**Given:**

Total race = 1200 m

A’s speed = 10 m/s

B headstart = 300 m ⇒ B runs 900 m

C headstart = 600 m ⇒ C runs 600 m

**Calculation:**

⇒ Time taken by A = 1200 / 10 = 120 s

⇒ B finishes 30 s after A

⇒ Time of B = 120 + 30 = 150 s

⇒ Speed of B = 900 / 150 = 6 m/s

⇒ C finishes 60 s after A

⇒ Time of C = 120 + 60 = 180 s

⇒ Speed of C = 600 / 180 = 3.33 ≈ 3.3 m/s

**∴ Speeds are B = 6 m/s and C = 3.3 m/s.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 

Headstart Concept

Subtract headstart from total distance

Time Difference

Add delay to A’s time

Formula

Speed = Distance / Time

questions.question: Which of the following dance forms is from Uttar Pradesh?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kathak**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kathak** is the primary classical dance form of **Northern India**, specifically originating and flourishing in the state of **Uttar Pradesh**. The term **Kathak** is derived from the **Sanskrit** word **'Katha'**, which translates to **'story'**, and the practitioners of this art are called **Kathakars** (storytellers).
 
• Historically, this dance form was performed by nomadic bards in **temples** who narrated mythological stories from the **Ramayana** and **Mahabharata** using facial expressions and hand gestures. During the **Bhakti Movement**, it evolved to include the tales of **Lord Krishna** and **Radha**. ***Hence, the option Kathak is correct.***
 
• Under the patronage of the **Mughal Emperors** and the **Nawabs of Lucknow**, **Kathak** transitioned from a temple ritual to a sophisticated **court dance**. This period introduced intricate **footwork (Tatkar)** and rapid **spins (Chakkars)**, blending **Persian** and **Indian** cultural elements.
 
• The dance is characterized by the use of **Ghungroos** (metallic bells) tied around the ankles, which are used to produce complex rhythmic patterns. Unlike other classical dances, **Kathak** is performed with **straight legs**, focusing on the movement of the ankles and feet.
 
• There are three main **Gharanas** or schools of **Kathak**: the **Lucknow Gharana** (famed for grace and **Abhinaya**), the **Jaipur Gharana** (known for powerful **Tandava** and technical footwork), and the **Banaras Gharana**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Bharatnatyam**: Originating from the state of **Tamil Nadu**, it is considered the **oldest** classical dance of India. It was traditionally known as **Sadir** and was performed by **Devadasis** in **South Indian temples**. Key features include the **Alarippu**, **Jatiswaram**, and **Tillana**. ***Hence, Bharatnatyam is from Tamil Nadu and not Uttar Pradesh.***
 
• **Odissi**: This dance form belongs to the state of **Odisha**. It is known for the **Tribhanga** posture, where the body is bent at the neck, torso, and knees. It traces its roots to the **Maharis** (female temple servants) and was famously mentioned in the **Natya Shastra**. ***Hence, Odissi is from Odisha and not Uttar Pradesh.***
 
• **Manipuri**: Hailing from the **North-Eastern** state of **Manipur**, this dance is deeply religious and revolves around the **Raslila**. It is distinctive for its **Pung Cholom** (drum dance) and the **cylindrical costume (Kumil)** worn by dancers. ***Hence, Manipuri is from Manipur and not Uttar Pradesh.***
 
• **Mohiniyattam**: A feminine classical dance from **Kerala**, it is performed solo by women. The name literally means **'Dance of the Enchantress'**, referring to the **Vishnu** avatar **Mohini**. It is known for its graceful, swaying movements.
 
• **Kuchipudi**: This dance-drama originated in the village of **Kuchipudi** in **Andhra Pradesh**. It often involves a unique feature where the dancer performs while standing on the rim of a **brass plate**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Sangeet Natak Akademi**, India’s national academy for music, dance, and drama, currently recognizes **8** classical dances of India. However, the **Ministry of Culture** also includes **Chhau** in the list, making it **9** classical dances.
 
• All Indian classical dances are rooted in the **Natya Shastra**, an ancient encyclopedic treatise on the performing arts written by **Bharata Muni** between **200 BCE** and **200 CE**.
 
• The legendary **Pandit Birju Maharaj** was the most prominent exponent of the **Lucknow Kalka-Bindadin Gharana** of **Kathak** and was awarded the **Padma Vibhushan** in **1986**.
 
• In **2000**, the **Sattriya** dance of **Assam** was the latest to be officially recognized as a classical dance form by the **Sangeet Natak Akademi**, having been introduced by the **Vaishnava** saint **Mahapurush Sankaradeva** in the **15th Century**.

questions.question: A shopkeeper sold two items for ₹10,000 each. He suffered a loss of 20% on one item and earned 20% profit on the other item. What is his profit or loss percentage in the whole transaction?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__ 

Loss 20% ⇒ SP = 80% of CP ⇒ CP₁ = 10000 / 0.8 = 12500

Profit 20% ⇒ SP = 120% of CP ⇒ CP₂ = 10000 / 1.2 = 8333.33

Total CP = 12500 + 8333.33 = 20833.33

Total SP = 20000

Loss = 833.33

Loss % = (833.33 / 20833.33) × 100 = 4%

**∴ Answer = 4% Loss**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__** 

**Given:**

SP of each item = ₹10000

Loss on one = 20%, Profit on other = 20%

**Formula used:**

SP = CP × (1 ± percentage/100)

**Calculation:**

⇒ For loss item:

SP = 0.8 × CP ⇒ CP = 10000 / 0.8 = 12500

⇒ For profit item:

SP = 1.2 × CP ⇒ CP = 10000 / 1.2 = 8333.33

⇒ Total CP = 12500 + 8333.33 = 20833.33

⇒ Total SP = 20000

⇒ Loss = 20833.33 − 20000 = 833.33

⇒ Loss % = (833.33 / 20833.33) × 100 = 4%

**∴ The correct answer is 4% loss.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 

Key Insight

Equal % gain and loss on same SP ⇒ always overall loss

Shortcut Formula

Net loss % = (x² / 100) when same SP ⇒ here = 20²/100 = 4%

questions.question: A person runs a concession stand at a basketball game and sells burgers and soft drinks. Each burger costs ₹15 and each soft drink costs ₹5. At the end, a total of ₹785 is earned by selling a total of 87 burgers and soft drinks combined. How many soft drinks are sold?

y = 87 − 35 = 52

questions.question: In an isosceles triangle ABC, the equal sides AB and AC are each 10 cm, and the base BC is 12 cm. Find the area of the triangle.
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__ 

Height splits base ⇒ 12/2 = 6

Use Pythagoras:

h = √(10² − 6²) = √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8

Area = (1/2) × base × height

= (1/2) × 12 × 8 = 48

**∴ Answer = 48 cm²**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__** 

**Given:**

AB = AC = 10 cm, BC = 12 cm

**Concept used:**

In an isosceles triangle, altitude bisects the base

**Calculation:**

⇒ Half base = 12/2 = 6

⇒ Using Pythagoras:

h² = 10² − 6²

h² = 100 − 36 = 64

h = 8 cm

⇒ Area = (1/2) × base × height

⇒ = (1/2) × 12 × 8 = 48 cm²

**∴ The correct answer is 48 cm².**

h² = hypotenuse² − base²

questions.question: What happens to light energy in interference and diffraction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is redistributed**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the phenomena of **interference** and **diffraction**, light energy is **redistributed**. This means that energy is simply moved from one place to another rather than being consumed or generated.
 
• According to the **Law of Conservation of Energy**, energy cannot be created or destroyed. In an interference pattern, the energy that disappears from the **dark regions** (destructive interference) reappears in the **bright regions** (constructive interference).
 
• In **interference**, the total energy in the superposition region is the sum of the energies of the individual waves. If we integrate the intensity over the entire fringe pattern, the **average intensity** remains the same as if the waves were not interfering. **Hence, option D is correct.**
 
• Light energy does not **reduce** or **decrease** in these processes. If it did, it would violate the principle of energy conservation. **Hence, statements A and C are incorrect.**
 
• Light energy does not **increase** because there is no external energy source adding to the system during the superposition of waves. **Hence, statement B is incorrect.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Interference of Light:** This occurs when two **coherent sources** of light (sources with a constant phase difference) overlap. A famous example is **Young’s Double Slit Experiment** conducted in **1801**.

 
 
• **Constructive Interference:** When waves meet in phase (crest to crest), the resultant **amplitude** is the sum of individual amplitudes, leading to **maxima** or bright fringes.
 
• **Destructive Interference:** When waves meet out of phase (crest to trough), the resultant amplitude is the difference between individual amplitudes, leading to **minima** or dark fringes.
 
 
 
• **Diffraction of Light:** This is the **bending of light** around the corners of an obstacle or an aperture. It is most prominent when the size of the obstacle is comparable to the **wavelength** of light.
 
 
• The **diffraction pattern** consists of a central bright fringe (central maximum) surrounded by alternating dark and bright fringes of **decreasing intensity**.
 
• Unlike interference, where all bright fringes are of equal intensity (in ideal conditions), in diffraction, the energy is spread such that the central maximum carries the most energy.
 
 
 
• **Intensity and Amplitude:** The **intensity (I)** of light is directly proportional to the **square of the amplitude (A)**. Mathematically, **I ∝ A²**. During redistribution, the variations in amplitude across space create the visible pattern.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mathematical Proof of Energy Conservation:** For two waves with intensities **I1** and **I2**, the resulting intensity at any point is **I = I1 + I2 + 2√(I1I2) cosφ**. When averaged over a full cycle of the phase difference **φ**, the **interference term** (2√(I1I2) cosφ) becomes **zero**, making the average intensity **I1 + I2**.
 
• **Coherence:** For a stable redistribution of energy (a steady interference pattern), the light sources must be **coherent**. Non-coherent sources (like two independent light bulbs) do not show visible redistribution because the phase difference changes too rapidly for the human eye to detect.
 
• **Applications:** The redistribution of light energy is utilized in **anti-reflective coatings** on camera lenses, **holography**, **spectrometers**, and **interferometers** (like the Michelson Interferometer) used to measure small distances or the **speed of light**.
 
• **Wave Nature:** Both interference and diffraction serve as definitive evidence for the **wave theory of light**, as proposed by **Thomas Young** and **Augustin-Jean Fresnel** in the early **19th century**.

questions.question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

**Statements:**

All grapes are lemons. No grape is a melon. No melon is a strawberry.

**Conclusions:**

(I) No lemon is a melon.

(II) No grape is a strawberry.
questions.solution:
Given Statements:

All grapes are lemons.

No grape is a melon.

No melon is a strawberry.

The least possible Venn diagram for the given statements is:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/639f132f29b4b70ae4f7ce65aef0210dd6638f2e61f1be22f723dcc9b4b8f913.png] 

Conclusions:

I. No lemon is a melon – **False**

(Because only grapes are restricted from melons; since lemons are a larger category, they can still overlap with melons in the area outside of the grape circle.)

II. No grape is a strawberry – **False**

(While grapes cannot be melons and melons cannot be strawberries, there is no direct restriction between grapes and strawberries; they could still overlap or be separate.)

So, neither conclusion I nor II follows.

**Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).**

questions.question: In a country with high informal employment and low social protection coverage, which policy is likely to be the most effective in both poverty alleviation and employment formalization?

options.text: Expand social insurance to informal sector

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Expand social insurance to informal sector**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Expanding social insurance to the informal sector** serves as a dual-purpose mechanism that provides a safety net while incentivizing the transition to the formal economy. By offering benefits like **pension** and **health insurance**, the government encourages **informal workers** to register, thereby initiating **employment formalization**. ***Hence, Statement A is correct.***
 
• **Universal Basic Income (UBI)** provides a flat **cash transfer** to all citizens regardless of employment status. While it is highly effective for **poverty alleviation**, it does not inherently provide a mechanism for **formalization** or link workers to the **labor market** structures. ***Hence, Statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Deregulating labor laws** is often intended to make hiring easier and reduce the **cost of compliance** for **employers**. However, in a country with already low **social protection coverage**, this often leads to further **precarity** and reduced **job security**, failing the **social protection** goal. ***Hence, Statement C is incorrect.***
 
• **Targeted food subsidies**, such as those under the **National Food Security Act (NFSA) 2013** in **India**, are vital for **nutrition** and **poverty relief** but have no direct impact on **employment formalization** or bringing workers into the **tax** or **social insurance** net. ***Hence, Statement D is incorrect.***
 
• The **formalization** process is crucial because the **informal sector** accounts for nearly **90%** of the **workforce** in developing nations like **India**, where workers lack **legal contracts** and **maternity benefits**.

• **Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-Dhan (PM-SYM):** Launched in **March 2019**, this is a **voluntary** and **contributory pension scheme** specifically for **unorganized workers**. It targets individuals with a **monthly income** of **Rs. 15,000** or less in the **age group** of **18 to 40 years**. It ensures a **minimum assured pension** of **Rs. 3,000 per month** after the **age** of **60 years**.
 
• **The e-Shram Portal:** Developed by the **Ministry of Labour & Employment** in **August 2021**, this is the first-ever **national database** of **unorganized workers** including **migrant workers**, **construction workers**, and **gig workers**. It facilitates the delivery of **social security schemes** and tracks **employment** trends.
 
• **ILO Recommendation No. 204:** This is a landmark **international standard** adopted by the **International Labour Organization (ILO)** in **2015**. It provides a **guideline** for member states to facilitate the **transition** from the **informal** to the **formal economy** while ensuring **decent work** and **worker rights**.
 
• **Social Security Code, 2020:** In **India**, this **act** aims to **universalize social security** for both **organized** and **unorganized sectors**. It seeks to consolidate **nine** previous **labor laws** and introduces provisions for **gig workers** and **platform workers** for the first time in **Indian legal history**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Missing Middle:** This term refers to a large segment of the **population** that is neither poor enough to qualify for **subsidized social assistance** (like **BPL cards**) nor wealthy enough to afford **private insurance** or be covered by **employer-based schemes**.
 
• **Economic Impact:** **Formalization** increases the **tax base** of a **country**, allowing for higher **public investment** in **infrastructure** and **education**. **Informal employment** often leads to low **productivity** and lack of **access to credit** from **formal financial institutions**.
 
• **Gender Perspective:** A high **percentage** of **women** are engaged in the **informal sector**, particularly in **domestic work** and **agriculture**. Expanding **social insurance** provides them with **maternity benefits** and **old-age security**, which are often absent in **informal arrangements**.
 
• **Administrative Challenges:** One of the main **features** of **expanding insurance** is the need for **digital literacy** and **biometric identification** (like **Aadhaar** in **India**) to prevent **leakages** and ensure **direct benefit transfer (DBT)**.

questions.question: When a Windows computer is in Sleep mode, which common user action will typically bring the system back to an active state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Moving the mouse**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sleep Mode** in **Windows** is a power-saving state that allows a computer to quickly resume full-power operation (typically within **2 to 5 seconds**) when a user wants to start working again. In this state, the current session and open applications are kept in the **Random Access Memory (RAM)** while other components like the hard drive and monitor are powered down.
 
• **Moving the mouse** or clicking a mouse button is one of the most common **interrupt triggers** that sends a signal to the **CPU** to exit the low-power state. This action tells the **Operating System** to restore power to the peripheral devices and the display. **Hence, option A is correct.**
 
• **Network time sync** is a background synchronization process using the **Network Time Protocol (NTP)**. While it ensures the system clock is accurate, it is a passive process that occurs while the system is already **awake** or in a **Modern Standby** mode; it does not typically "wake" a traditional sleeping PC for the user. **Hence, option B is incorrect.**
 
• A **BIOS update** (Basic Input/Output System) is a critical low-level firmware procedure that requires the computer to be fully **active** or in the middle of a **reboot** cycle. A computer cannot perform a firmware update while it is in **Sleep mode**, as the processor is not executing standard instruction sets during that time. **Hence, option C is incorrect.**
 
• If a **battery is fully drained** while a laptop is in sleep mode, the system does not become "active." Instead, **Windows** typically triggers a **critical battery alarm** and automatically moves the data from **RAM** to the **Hard Drive/SSD** (entering **Hibernation**) or simply shuts down to prevent hardware damage. **Hence, option D is incorrect.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI):** This is an open industry standard that **Windows** uses for power management. The "Sleep" state is technically known as the **S3 state**. In this state, the **PSU (Power Supply Unit)** stops providing power to most components except for the **RAM**, which must remain powered to retain the system's current data.
 
• **Sleep vs. Hibernation:** While **Sleep** (S3) keeps data in the volatile **RAM** for a near-instant wake, **Hibernation** (S4) saves the data to the non-volatile **Hard Disk**. Hibernation uses **zero power** and is common in **laptops** to save **battery life** over long periods of inactivity, whereas Sleep is preferred for short breaks.
 
• **Wake-on-LAN (WOL):** This is a **networking feature** that allows a computer to be turned on or awakened by a **network message** (called a **Magic Packet**). This is widely used by **IT administrators** in large **organizations** to perform maintenance on computers remotely during **night hours**.
 
• **Device Manager Settings:** Users can customize which devices wake the computer. Under **Device Manager**, by selecting the **Properties** of a **Keyboard** or **HID-compliant mouse**, one can check or uncheck the option **"Allow this device to wake the computer"**. This is useful for preventing accidental wakes by pets or vibrations.
 
• **Hybrid Sleep:** This **feature**, primarily designed for **desktop computers**, combines Sleep and Hibernation. It puts open documents and programs in **RAM** and on the **hard disk**. If a **power failure** occurs, **Windows** can restore your work from the **hard disk**; if power remains, the system wakes instantly from **RAM**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Modern Standby (S0 Low Power Idle):** Introduced with **Windows 10**, this allows the PC to stay connected to the **Internet** while in a low-power state, similar to a **smartphone**. This enables functions like **Cortana** or **Email syncing** to happen in the background, though **moving the mouse** remains the standard user-initiated wake action.
 
• **Power Consumption:** **Sleep mode** typically consumes about **1 to 5 watts** of power, whereas a fully **active PC** can consume anywhere from **60 to 500 watts** depending on the hardware and load.

questions.question: What does the Environment Audit Rules, 2025, aim to establish across India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A framework for environmental accountability**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Environment Audit Rules, 2025**, are designed to streamline the process of monitoring industrial impact on the ecosystem by establishing a formal **framework for environmental accountability**. This initiative ensures that both **public and private sector** entities are held responsible for their **carbon footprint** and **resource consumption**.
 
• These rules were formulated under the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC)** to update the existing **Environmental Audit** mechanisms that have been in place since the **1990s**. The **2025** version introduces more **stringent reporting standards** and **mandatory third-party verifications**.
 
• The primary **function** of these rules is to mandate that industries provide an annual **Environmental Statement** for each financial year ending on the **31st of March**. This document must detail **water consumption**, **raw material usage**, and **pollutant discharge** levels.
 
• The **application** of these rules extends to all "red" and "orange" category industries as classified by the **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)**, aiming to integrate **sustainable development** goals into the core business operations of **Indian enterprises**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Environment Protection Act, 1986**:

 
 
• The **Environment Audit Rules** derive their legal authority from **Section 6** and **Section 25** of the **Environment Protection Act, 1986**. This **Act** serves as the umbrella legislation for environmental **regulation** and **protection** in **India**.
 
 
 
• **Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR)**:
 
 
• The **2025 framework** is closely aligned with the **BRSR** norms introduced by the **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)**. While **BRSR** focuses on **top 1000 listed companies**, the **Environment Audit Rules** target a broader range of **manufacturing** and **processing units** based on their **pollution potential**.
 
 
 
• **Role of the National Green Tribunal (NGT)**:
 
 
• The **NGT**, established in **2010**, plays a crucial role in adjudicating disputes arising from **audit failures**. Non-compliance with the **2025 Rules** can lead to **heavy penalties** or the **closure of industrial units** as per **NGT** directives.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Global Standards**:
 
 
• The **Indian** framework incorporates elements from the **ISO 14001** (Environmental Management Systems) but remains **statutory** rather than voluntary. It emphasizes **data-driven governance** to meet **international commitments** such as the **Paris Agreement** and **COP26** goals.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Audit Components**: The **audit** process includes **energy audits**, **waste management audits**, and **occupational health and safety** assessments. Entities must report **numerical values** for **effluent treatment plant (ETP)** efficiency and **air emission** levels.
 
• **Certification**: The rules specify that audits must be performed by **Environmental Auditors** registered with the **Quality Council of India (QCI)** or the **National Accreditation Board for Education and Training (NABET)**.
 
• **Digital Integration**: A significant **feature** of the **2025** rules is the transition to a **paperless reporting system**. All **Environmental Statements** must be uploaded to the **Parivesh Portal**, a **Single-Window Integrated Environmental Management System**.
 
• **Year of Implementation**: While the rules are titled for **2025**, the **transition period** for existing industries usually spans **6 to 12 months**, making **2026** the first full **compliance year** for **data submission**.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a peninsular river?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ganga**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ganga**: It is a **Himalayan river** that originates from the **Gangotri Glacier** near **Gaumukh** in the **Uttarkashi** district of **Uttarakhand**. It is not part of the peninsular river system. ***Hence, this option is the correct answer.***
 
• **Narmada**: It is a major **peninsular river** that flows **westwards** through a **rift valley** between the **Vindhya** and **Satpura** ranges. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect as it is a peninsular river.***
 
• **Krishna**: It is the **second-largest east-flowing peninsular river**, originating near **Mahabaleshwar** in **Maharashtra**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect as it is a peninsular river.***
 
• **Godavari**: It is the **largest peninsular river** system in **India**, often referred to as the **Dakshin Ganga**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect as it is a peninsular river.***
 
• The **Ganga** river basin is the largest in **India**, covering about **8.6 lakh sq. km** and flowing through **India** and **Bangladesh** for a total length of **2,525 km**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Ganga River System**:

 
 
• The river is formed by the confluence of the **Alaknanda** and **Bhagirathi** at **Devprayag**.
 
• It enters the plains at **Haridwar** and receives several tributaries like the **Yamuna**, **Ghaghara**, **Gandak**, and **Kosi**.
 
• The **Yamuna**, its largest tributary, originates from the **Yamunotri Glacier** and meets the Ganga at **Prayagraj** (Allahabad).
 
• The river eventually empties into the **Bay of Bengal**, forming the **Sundarbans Delta**, the largest delta in the world, along with the **Brahmaputra**.
 
 
 
• **The Peninsular River System**:
 
 
• These rivers are much **older** than the Himalayan rivers and are mostly **non-perennial** or seasonal, as their flow is dependent on **rainfall**.
 
• The main water divide in Peninsular India is formed by the **Western Ghats**, which run from north to south close to the western coast.
 
• Major east-flowing rivers include the **Mahanadi**, **Godavari**, **Krishna**, and **Cauvery**, which drain into the **Bay of Bengal** and form **deltas**.
 
• Major west-flowing rivers are the **Narmada** and **Tapi**, which flow through **rift valleys** and form **estuaries** instead of deltas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison of River Types**:

 
 
• **Himalayan Rivers**: These include the **Indus**, **Ganga**, and **Brahmaputra**. They are **perennial** (flow year-round) because they receive water from **glaciers** and **monsoon rainfall**. They have **long courses** and perform intensive **erosional activity**.
 
• **Peninsular Rivers**: These are **seasonal** and have **shorter and shallower courses** compared to their Himalayan counterparts. Their flow is significantly reduced during the **dry season**.
 
 
 
• **Specific Statistics**:
 
 
• The **Godavari** has a length of **1,465 km** and its basin covers parts of **Maharashtra**, **Madhya Pradesh**, **Chhattisgarh**, **Odisha**, and **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• The **Narmada** travels a distance of about **1,312 km** before reaching the **Gulf of Khambhat**.
 
• The **Krishna** river flows for **1,400 km** and is vital for irrigation in **South India**.

questions.question: Three positive integers, A, B, and C, satisfy the following conditions: HCF(A,B) = 12, HCF(B,C) = 18, HCF(A,C) = 6 and LCM(A,B,C) = 1080. If A = 12x, B = 36y, and C = 18z, where x, y, and z are pairwise coprime positive integers, then the minimum possible value of A + B + C is:
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

LCM(A, B, C) = 1080 = 2³ × 3³ × 5.

Since HCF(A, B) = 12, HCF(B, C) = 18, and HCF(A, C) = 6, the prime factors must be distributed such that x, y, and z are pairwise coprime.

Testing x = 2, y = 3, z = 5 (all pairwise coprime):

A = 12 × 2 = 24, B = 36 × 3 = 108, C = 18 × 5 = 90.

Check: LCM(24, 108, 90) = 1080 and HCFs are correct. Sum = 24 + 108 + 90 = 222.

**∴ The correct answer is 222.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

Given:

A = 12x, B = 36y, C = 18z

HCF(A, B) = 12, HCF(B, C) = 18, HCF(A, C) = 6

LCM(A, B, C) = 1080 = 2³ × 3³ × 5

Formula used: LCM of numbers is the product of the highest powers of all prime factors involved.

 A = 12 × x B = 36 × y C = 18 × z LCM Factor 2³ 
 LCM Factor 3³ 
 LCM Factor 5 
 Min Sum A+B+C = 222 

Prime factorization of constants:

A = 2² × 3¹ × x

B = 2² × 3² × y

C = 2¹ × 3² × z

To satisfy LCM = 2³ × 3³ × 5¹:

⇒ max(2, 2, 1, v₂(x), v₂(y), v₂(z)) = 3

⇒ max(1, 2, 2, v₃(x), v₃(y), v₃(z)) = 3

⇒ max(v₅(x), v₅(y), v₅(z)) = 1

Using the pairwise coprime condition and HCF constraints:

⇒ For v₂ = 3, we can set x = 2 (since A already has 2², 12 × 2 = 24 has 2³).

⇒ For v₃ = 3, we can set y = 3 (since B already has 3², 36 × 3 = 108 has 3³).

⇒ For v₅ = 1, we can set z = 5 (since C is 18 × 5 = 90).

⇒ (x, y, z) = (2, 3, 5) are pairwise coprime.

⇒ A = 12 × 2 = 24

⇒ B = 36 × 3 = 108

⇒ C = 18 × 5 = 90

⇒ A + B + C = 24 + 108 + 90 = 222.

**∴ The correct answer is 222.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

LCM and HCF Relationship

For any three numbers A, B, and C, LCM(A, B, C) × HCF(A, B) × HCF(B, C) × HCF(A, C) is not necessarily equal to A × B × C × HCF(A, B, C), unlike the case for two numbers.

Pairwise Coprime Integers

A set of integers is pairwise coprime if the HCF of every possible pair in the set is 1. If HCF(x, y) = 1, HCF(y, z) = 1, and HCF(x, z) = 1, then LCM(x, y, z) = x × y × z.

Prime Power in LCM

The exponent of a prime p in the LCM of a set of numbers is the maximum of the exponents of p in the prime factorizations of those numbers.

questions.question: Which of the following nationalists co-founded and became the president of the Congress-Khilafat Swarajya Party, after a fall off with the Indian National Congress?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chittaranjan Das**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Congress-Khilafat Swarajya Party**, commonly known as the **Swaraj Party**, was formed on **January 1, 1923**.
 
• The party was established following the **Gaya Session** of the **Indian National Congress** held in **December 1922**, where a conflict arose between the "Pro-Changers" and the "No-Changers."
 
• **Chittaranjan Das**, also known as **Deshbandhu**, served as the **President** of the newly formed party, while **Motilal Nehru** took the role of one of its **Secretaries**.
 
• The primary objective of the party was to contest elections for the **Legislative Councils** established under the **Government of India Act 1919** and to "wreck the reforms from within" by obstructing official business.
 
• This move was a response to the suspension of the **Non-Cooperation Movement** by **Mahatma Gandhi** in **February 1922** following the **Chauri Chaura incident**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chittaranjan Das (1870–1925):**

 
 
• He was a distinguished **lawyer** from **Bengal** who famously defended **Aurobindo Ghosh** in the **Alipore Bomb Case** of **1908**.
 
• He was known for his selfless service and was given the title **Deshbandhu** (Friend of the Nation).
 
• He was elected as the **President** of the **Ahmedabad Session** of Congress in **1921**, though he was in jail at the time.
 
 
 
• **Motilal Nehru (1861–1931):**
 
 
• A prominent **lawyer** and **politician** from **Allahabad**, he served as the **President** of the **Indian National Congress** twice, in **1919** (Amritsar) and **1928** (Calcutta).
 
• He was the father of **Jawaharlal Nehru** and the author of the **Nehru Report (1928)**, which was the first major attempt by Indians to draft a constitution.
 
 
 
• **Hakim Ajmal Khan:**
 
 
• He was another prominent **co-founder** of the **Swaraj Party** and a key figure in the **Khilafat Movement**.
 
• He served as the **President** of the **Congress** in **1921** as a substitute for **C.R. Das**.
 
 
 
• **Belgaum Session (1924):**
 
 
• To avoid a split in the **Congress** similar to the **Surat Split of 1907**, **Mahatma Gandhi** reached a compromise with the Swarajists.
 
• The **Swaraj Party** was allowed to work within the **Congress** as its integral part, focusing on council entry.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Pro-Changers vs. No-Changers:**

 
 
• **Pro-Changers:** Leaders like **C.R. Das**, **Motilal Nehru**, and **Vithalbhai Patel** who advocated for ending the boycott of legislative councils.
 
• **No-Changers:** Leaders like **C. Rajagopalachari**, **Vallabhbhai Patel**, and **Rajendra Prasad** who wanted to stick to **Gandhian** methods of constructive work outside the government.
 
 
 
• **Performance in 1923 Elections:**
 
 
• The **Swaraj Party** performed remarkably well in the **November 1923** elections, winning **42 out of 101** elected seats in the **Central Legislative Assembly**.
 
• In **1925**, **Vithalbhai Patel** became the first Indian **Speaker** (President) of the **Central Legislative Assembly**, marking a significant victory for the party.
 
 
 
• **Decline of the Party:**
 
 
• The party suffered a major setback following the sudden death of **Chittaranjan Das** in **June 1925**.

questions.question: What administrative change characterized the political structure of post-Gupta India?

options.text: Replacement of kingship with religious councils
Formation of a central bureaucracy under one emperor
Rise of smaller kingdoms under hereditary rulers
Introduction of democratic village assemblies across India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rise of smaller kingdoms under hereditary rulers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The decline of the **Gupta Empire** around **550 CE** marked a transition from a centralized imperial structure to a decentralized political landscape in India. This era witnessed the emergence of numerous regional powers that asserted their independence.
 
• Replacement of kingship with religious councils: While religious institutions like monasteries and temples gained land and influence, the basic unit of political power remained the monarchy, and religious councils did not replace kings as supreme administrative heads. **Hence, statement A is incorrect.**
 
• Formation of a central bureaucracy under one emperor: The post-Gupta period was actually characterized by the breakdown of central authority rather than the creation of a new, unified bureaucracy. Power became fragmented among local lords. **Hence, statement B is incorrect.**
 
• Rise of smaller kingdoms under hereditary rulers: After the **Guptas**, various dynasties such as the **Pushyabhutis** (Vardhanas), **Maitrakas**, **Maukharis**, and later the **Rajputs** established local sovereignty where administrative and military power was held by hereditary elites. **Hence, statement C is correct.**
 
• Introduction of democratic village assemblies across India: While certain regions like the far south (under the **Cholas** later on) had robust village assemblies like the **Ur** and **Sabha**, this was not the defining "administrative change" for the whole of post-Gupta India's political structure. **Hence, statement D is incorrect.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Feudalization of Administration:** The most significant feature of this period was the rise of the **Samanta system**. Kings granted land to officers and Brahmins in lieu of cash salaries. These grantees, known as **Samantas**, eventually became powerful enough to challenge the central authority and establish their own **hereditary** lineages.
 
• **Harshavardhana of Kannauj:** Ruling from **606 to 647 CE**, **Harsha** was the last major ruler who attempted to unify Northern India. However, his empire was more of a loose confederation of **feudatories** rather than a tightly knit centralized state like the **Mauryas**. His capital was shifted from **Thanesar** to **Kannauj**, which became the political center of gravity.
 
• **Regional Dynasties:** The period saw the rise of the **Chalukyas of Vatapi** in the Deccan and the **Pallavas of Kanchi** in the South. These kingdoms engaged in constant warfare over fertile river valleys like the **Krishna-Godaveri** delta, reflecting the competitive nature of regional **hereditary** politics.
 
• **Land Grants and Economy:** The practice of **Agrahara** (land grants to Brahmins) and **Brahmadeya** became widespread. This led to a ruralization of the economy as trade declined following the fall of the **Roman Empire** and the **Huna invasions**, forcing the political structure to rely heavily on **land revenue** and local agrarian control.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Tripartite Struggle:** Following the death of **Harsha**, the city of **Kannauj** became the symbol of sovereignty. This led to the **Tripartite Struggle** between the **Palas of Bengal**, the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** of the West, and the **Rashtrakutas** of the Deccan during the **8th to 10th centuries**.
 
• **Bureaucratic Shifts:** Administrative posts like the **Mahasandhivigrahika** (Minister of War and Peace) and **Kumaramatyas** became increasingly **hereditary**, further weakening the king's ability to reshuffle his administration and strengthening the local nobility.
 
• **Huna Invasions:** The frequent **Huna** incursions in the **5th and 6th centuries** disrupted the **Gupta** trade routes and treasury, providing the catalyst for provincial governors to declare themselves independent **Maharajas**.

questions.question: What is the atomicity of a molecule of oxygen (O₂)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Atomicity** is defined as the **total number of atoms** present in one molecule of an element, compound, or substance.
 
• Oxygen naturally exists as a **diatomic molecule**, represented by the chemical formula **O₂**. This means that **two atoms** of oxygen are chemically bonded together to form one stable molecule. ***Hence, the statement regarding atomicity being 2 is correct.***
 
• The atomicity of **4** is typically seen in elements like **Phosphorus (P₄)**, which is a tetratomic molecule. ***Hence, the option suggesting 4 is incorrect.***
 
• The atomicity of **3** represents a **triatomic molecule**, such as **Ozone (O₃)**, which is an allotrope of oxygen but is not the standard oxygen molecule used in respiration. ***Hence, the option suggesting 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The atomicity of **1** represents **monoatomic** elements, which are primarily **Noble Gases** like **Helium (He)** and **Argon (Ar)** that do not usually form bonds with other atoms of the same element. ***Hence, the option suggesting 1 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Monoatomic Elements:** These consist of single atoms. Most **metals** (in their solid state representation) and **noble gases** (Group 18 elements) like **Neon (Ne)** and **Krypton (Kr)** exhibit an atomicity of **1**.
 
• **Diatomic Molecules:** Apart from **Oxygen (O₂)**, other common diatomic molecules include **Hydrogen (H₂)**, **Nitrogen (N₂)**, **Fluorine (F₂)**, **Chlorine (Cl₂)**, **Bromine (Br₂)**, and **Iodine (I₂)**. These are often remembered using the mnemonic "Have No Fear Of Ice Cold Beer".
 
• **Triatomic and Polyatomic Molecules:** **Ozone (O₃)** is a triatomic molecule that forms a protective layer in the **Earth's stratosphere** to absorb harmful **UV radiation**. **Sulfur** usually exists as **S₈**, making it a **polyatomic (octatomic)** molecule.
 
• **Chemical Nature of Oxygen:** **Oxygen** has an **atomic number** of **8** and its electronic configuration is **2, 6**. To achieve a stable octet, two oxygen atoms share **two pairs of electrons**, forming a **double covalent bond**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Discovery:** Oxygen was independently discovered by **Carl Wilhelm Scheele** in **1772** and **Joseph Priestley** in **1774**. However, **Antoine Lavoisier** was the one who named it in **1777**.
 
• **Abundance:** Oxygen is the **most abundant element** in the **Earth's crust**, making up about **46.6%** of its mass, and it constitutes approximately **21%** of the **Earth's atmosphere** by volume.
 
• **Applications:** Oxygen is crucial for **aerobic respiration** in almost all living organisms. In industrial settings, it is used in **steel manufacturing**, **welding (oxy-acetylene torches)**, and as **rocket propellant** in its liquid form (**LOX**).
 
• **Allotropes:** Oxygen has two main allotropes: **Dioxygen (O₂)**, which is essential for life, and **Ozone (O₃)**, which is highly reactive and can be toxic at ground level but vital in the upper atmosphere.

questions.question: Right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years is provided under which Article?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 21A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 21A** of the **Constitution of India** declares that the **State** shall provide **free and compulsory education** to all children in the **age group of six to fourteen years** in such a manner as the State may, by law, determine. ***Hence, Option D is correct.***
 
• This provision was not part of the original Constitution but was inserted by the **86th Constitutional Amendment Act** in the year **2002** to make education a **Fundamental Right**.
 
• The term **"Compulsory"** casts an obligation on the **appropriate government** and local authorities to provide and ensure admission, attendance, and completion of **elementary education** by all children in the **6-14 age group**.
 
• The term **"Free"** signifies that no child shall be liable to pay any kind of fee or charges or expenses which may prevent him or her from pursuing and completing elementary education.
 
• Consequent to this amendment, the **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009** was enacted to provide the legal framework for the implementation of **Article 21A**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 45:**

 
 
• This is a **Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP)**. Initially, it provided for free and compulsory education for all children until they complete the age of **14 years**.
 
• However, after the **86th Amendment Act (2002)**, its scope was changed to **"Early Childhood Care and Education"** for all children until they complete the age of **six years**. ***Hence, Option B is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Article 51A(k):**
 
 
• This falls under **Fundamental Duties** (Part IV-A). The **86th Amendment Act** added a new fundamental duty under **Article 51A**.
 
• It states that it shall be the duty of every **citizen of India** who is a **parent or guardian** to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of **six and fourteen years**. ***Hence, Option A is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Article 19:**
 
 
• This Article guarantees **six fundamental freedoms** to the citizens of India, including **freedom of speech and expression**, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession.
 
• It does not specifically deal with the right to primary education. ***Hence, Option C is incorrect.***
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The RTE Act, 2009:** This Act became operative on **1st April 2010**. India became one of the **135 countries** in the world to make education a fundamental right for every child.
 
• **Judicial Precedents:** Before the amendment, the **Supreme Court** in the **Mohini Jain vs. State of Karnataka (1992)** and **Unnikrishnan vs. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)** cases ruled that the **Right to Education** is a concomitant to the **Fundamental Rights** enshrined under **Article 21** (Right to Life).
 
• **Provisions of the Act:** The **RTE Act** mandates a **25% reservation** for disadvantaged groups and **economically weaker sections (EWS)** in all private unaided schools.
 
• **Monitoring:** The **National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR)** is the designated body to monitor the implementation of the rights provided under the Act.
 
• **Exemptions:** It is important to note that **Minority Educational Institutions** (both religious and linguistic) are exempt from the **25% reservation** quota as per various **Supreme Court** judgments to protect their rights under **Article 30**.

questions.question: In which year was the report of Methodology for Measurement of Poverty in India submitted by the Dr. C Rangarajan Committee?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Expert Group** to Review the **Methodology for Measurement of Poverty**, chaired by **Dr. C. Rangarajan**, was constituted by the **Planning Commission** in **June 2012**.
 
• The committee submitted its final report in **July 2014**, providing a revised framework for identifying the poor in **India**.
 
• The **Rangarajan Committee** estimated that the poverty ratio in **India** was **29.5%** in the year **2011-12**, which meant approximately **363 million** people were living below the poverty line.
 
• It recommended a higher poverty line than the previous **Tendulkar Committee**, setting the monthly per capita expenditure at **₹972** for **rural areas** and **₹1407** for **urban areas** at **2011-12** prices.
 
• The methodology adopted by the committee moved away from a solely calorie-based approach to a more comprehensive basket of goods including **nutrition**, **clothing**, **house rent**, **conveyance**, and **education**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Methodology of Rangarajan Committee:**

 
 
• The group based its estimates on the **NSSO 68th Round** survey data on **Household Consumer Expenditure** for the year **2011-12**.

• **Evolution of Poverty Estimation in India:**

 
 
• **Alagh Committee (1979):** Established the first poverty line based on **nutritional requirements** (**2400 kcal** rural and **2100 kcal** urban).
 
• **Lakdawala Committee (1993):** Introduced state-specific poverty lines and used the **Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL)** and **Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW)**.
 
• **NITI Aayog:** Following the dissolution of the **Planning Commission** in **2014**, **NITI Aayog** now acts as the nodal agency for poverty estimation and monitoring through its **Task Force on Elimination of Poverty**.

questions.question: Which gases act as the main greenhouse gases with rising atmospheric concentrations?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Greenhouse Gases (GHGs)** are components of the atmosphere that contribute to the **greenhouse effect** by absorbing and emitting radiant energy within the thermal infrared range. The primary greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere include **Carbon Dioxide (CO2)**, **Methane (CH4)**, and **Nitrous Oxide (N2O)**.
 
• **Carbon dioxide (CO2)** is the most significant long-lived greenhouse gas in Earth's atmosphere. Since the **Industrial Revolution**, anthropogenic emissions—primarily from the **use of fossil fuels** and **deforestation**—have caused its atmospheric concentration to rise significantly. ***Hence, the inclusion of Carbon dioxide in the answer is correct.***
 
• **Methane (CH4)** is a potent greenhouse gas with a **Global Warming Potential (GWP)** much higher than CO2. It is emitted during the production and transport of **coal**, **natural gas**, and **oil**, as well as from **livestock** (enteric fermentation) and **agricultural practices**. ***Hence, the inclusion of Methane in the answer is correct.***
 
• **Nitrous oxide (N2O)** is emitted during **agricultural** and **industrial activities**, combustion of **fossil fuels** and **solid waste**, as well as during treatment of **wastewater**. It has a long atmospheric life and a high GWP. ***Hence, the inclusion of Nitrous oxide in the answer is correct.***
 
• Gases like **Nitrogen (N2)**, **Oxygen (O2)**, and **Argon (Ar)** are not greenhouse gases because they consist of symmetrical **diatomic molecules** or single atoms that do not absorb infrared radiation. ***Hence, options containing these gases are incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kyoto Protocol:** This international treaty, adopted in **1997**, initially identified six main greenhouse gases that required emission reductions: **Carbon dioxide (CO2)**, **Methane (CH4)**, **Nitrous oxide (N2O)**, **Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs)**, **Perfluorocarbons (PFCs)**, and **Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6)**.
 
• **Atmospheric Composition:** Earth's atmosphere is primarily composed of **Nitrogen (78%)** and **Oxygen (21%)**. While they are the most abundant, they do not contribute to the greenhouse effect. Trace gases, including GHGs, make up less than **1%** of the atmosphere but have a profound impact on global temperature.
 
• **Global Warming Potential (GWP):** This is a measure of how much energy the emissions of **1 ton** of a gas will absorb over a given period (usually **100 years**), relative to the emissions of **1 ton of carbon dioxide**. **Methane** has a GWP of approximately **25-28**, while **Nitrous Oxide** has a GWP of around **265-298**.
 
• **Industrial and Synthetic Gases:** Fluorinated gases like **HFCs**, **PFCs**, and **SF6** are man-made and used in applications like **refrigeration** and **electronics manufacturing**. Although present in small concentrations, they are extremely potent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Water Vapor:** It is actually the most abundant greenhouse gas in the atmosphere. However, it is not directly increased by human activity; instead, its concentration depends on the **atmospheric temperature**, creating a **feedback loop**.
 
• **Concentration Milestones:** Atmospheric **Carbon dioxide** concentrations have surpassed **400 parts per million (ppm)** in recent years, a level not seen in millions of years. This rise is primarily attributed to the **burning of fossil fuels** since the year **1750**.
 
• **Impact of Deforestation:** Forests act as **carbon sinks**. When they are cleared or burned, they release stored carbon back into the atmosphere as **CO2**, exacerbating the greenhouse effect.
 
• **Agricultural Impact:** **Rice cultivation** and **cattle rearing** are the largest human-related sources of **Methane** emissions globally.

questions.question: As per the Constitution of India, Article 182 deals with which of the following?

options.text: Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the State Legislative Council

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the State Legislative Council**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 182** of the **Constitution of India** specifically provides for the **Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council**. It mandates that every **State** having a **Legislative Council** (Vidhan Parishad) shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the Council to be respectively **Chairman** and **Deputy Chairman** thereof. ***Hence, statement D is correct.***
 
• The **Chairman** acts as the presiding officer of the house. In the absence of the **Chairman**, the **Deputy Chairman** performs the duties of the office.
 
• This **Article** ensures the continuity of the leadership within the upper house of the **State Legislature**. If the office of the **Chairman** or **Deputy Chairman** becomes vacant, the **Council** is constitutionally obligated to choose another member to fill the vacancy.
 
• Unlike the **Speaker** of the **Legislative Assembly**, who is elected by the lower house, the **Chairman** is elected solely by the members of the **Legislative Council** from among its own members.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Composition of State Legislative Assemblies**: This is addressed under **Article 170**. It states that the **Legislative Assembly** of each State shall consist of not more than **500**, and not less than **60**, members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the State. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect in the context of Article 182.***
 
• **Disqualification for membership**: The criteria for the disqualification of members of either House of the State Legislature are laid down in **Article 191**. Reasons for disqualification include holding an **office of profit**, being of **unsound mind**, **insolvency**, or not being a **citizen of India**. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect in the context of Article 182.***
 
• **Special address by the Governor**: This provision is found in **Article 176**. The **Governor** addresses the **Legislative Assembly** (or both Houses in bicameral states) at the commencement of the first session after each **general election** and at the commencement of the first session of each **year**. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect in the context of Article 182.***
 
• **Article 171**: This article deals with the **Composition of the Legislative Councils**. It specifies that the total number of members in the **Legislative Council** of a State shall not exceed **one-third** of the total number of members in the **Legislative Assembly** of that State, but shall in no case be less than **40**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Vacation and Resignation (Article 183)**: A member holding office as **Chairman** or **Deputy Chairman** of a **Legislative Council** shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Council. The **Chairman** may resign by writing to the **Deputy Chairman**, and the **Deputy Chairman** may resign by writing to the **Chairman**.
 
• **Removal**: They can be removed from office by a resolution of the **Council** passed by a **majority** of all the then members of the Council, provided that at least **14 days' notice** has been given of the intention to move the resolution.
 
• **States with Legislative Councils**: Currently, only **six states** in India have a bicameral legislature (both Vidhan Sabha and Vidhan Parishad). These are **Andhra Pradesh**, **Bihar**, **Karnataka**, **Maharashtra**, **Telangana**, and **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• **Role of the Chairman**: The **Chairman** has the power to adjourn the **House** or suspend the meeting in the absence of a **quorum**. The **Chairman** does not vote in the first instance but exercises a **casting vote** in the case of an equality of votes.

questions.question: The Right to Property was removed from Part III of the Indian Constitution and added to _____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Part XII**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Right to Property** was originally a **Fundamental Right** in the Indian Constitution, protected under **Article 19(1)(f)** and **Article 31** in **Part III**.
 
• The **44th Amendment Act, 1978**, passed during the tenure of the **Janata Party** government, abolished the Right to Property as a fundamental right. *Hence, the statement that it was removed from Part III is correct.*
 
• Following its removal from Part III, it was re-introduced as a **Constitutional Right** (or legal right) under **Article 300A**.
 
• This new article, **Article 300A**, is located in **Part XII** of the Constitution, specifically under the chapter titled '**Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits**'. *Hence, the statement that it was added to Part XII is correct.*
 
• The primary objective of this shift was to prevent property rights from becoming a hurdle in the implementation of **land reforms** and other **socialist policies** aimed at equitable distribution of wealth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 300A:** This article states that "no person shall be deprived of his property save by **authority of law**." This means that while the state can still acquire private property, it must do so by following a valid law passed by the **legislature**, rather than through executive action alone.
 
• **Status as a Legal Right:** Unlike Fundamental Rights, a **legal right** does not allow a citizen to directly approach the **Supreme Court** under **Article 32** for its violation. However, a person can still seek remedy through a **High Court** under **Article 226**.
 
• **Compensation:** After the **44th Amendment**, the state is not constitutionally obligated to pay "compensation" for acquired property except in two specific instances: when the state acquires property of a **minority educational institution** or land held by a person under **personal cultivation** within the statutory ceiling limits.
 
• **Historical Context:** The conflict between the **Judiciary** and the **Executive** over property rights was a defining feature of Indian politics in the **1950s**, **1960s**, and **1970s**, leading to landmark cases like **Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar** and the **Bank Nationalization case**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights (Part III):** These are **justiciable** rights that are fundamental to the development of an individual and are protected by the basic structure of the Constitution. Before **1978**, there were **seven** fundamental rights; currently, there are only **six**.
 
• **Janata Party Government:** The amendment was spearheaded by Prime Minister **Morarji Desai** in **1978** to reverse several changes made during the **Emergency** and to settle the long-standing debate on property acquisition.
 
• **Part XII Structure:** This part of the Constitution deals with **Finance** (Articles 264-291), **Borrowing** (Articles 292-293), **Property, Contracts, Rights, Liabilities, Obligations and Suits** (Articles 294-300), and the **Right to Property** (Article 300A).

__
 
• The **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** was constituted under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**, to monitor and evaluate the implementation of legal aid programs and to lay down policies and principles for making legal services available under the **Act**.
 
• The **Legal Services Authorities Act** officially came into force on **9th November 1995** to establish a nationwide uniform network for providing free and competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society.

• The **Chief Justice of India** serves as the **Patron-in-Chief** of **NALSA**, while the **second senior-most Judge** of the **Supreme Court of India** acts as the **Executive Chairman**.
 
• In every **State**, a **State Legal Services Authority (SLSA)** has been constituted to give effect to the policies and directions of **NALSA** and to give free legal services to the people and conduct **Lok Adalats** in the **State**.

__
 
• **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (Option A)**: This **Act** provides for the statutory constitution of legal services authorities at the **National**, **State**, and **District** levels. It ensures that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities. ***Hence, this statement is correct.***
 
• **Advocates Act, 1961 (Option B)**: This **Act** was enacted to amend and consolidate the law relating to legal practitioners and to provide for the constitution of **Bar Councils** and an **All-India Bar**. It regulates the professional conduct of advocates but did not establish **NALSA**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Option C)**: Under **Section 304** of the **CrPC**, the court provides legal aid to an accused person if they do not have sufficient means to engage a lawyer at the **State's** expense. While it supports the concept of legal aid, the administrative body **NALSA** was not created by this code. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Legal Aid and Advice Act, 1972 (Option D)**: While various committees on legal aid were formed in the **1970s** (like the **Krishna Iyer Committee** in **1973**), there is no specific central **Act** by this name that serves as the founding legislation for **NALSA**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

• **Eligibility**: According to **Section 12** of the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**, eligible persons include **Women and Children**, members of **SC/ST**, **Industrial workmen**, victims of **mass disasters**, **violence**, **floods**, or **disabled persons**.

questions.question: Which shortcut is used to undo the last action?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ctrl+Z**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ctrl+Z** is the standard keyboard shortcut used to **undo** the last action performed in most software applications, including **Microsoft Windows**, **macOS** (where it is Command+Z), and various **Linux** distributions.
 
• The function of this shortcut is to **revert** the state of a document or system to the immediate previous step, allowing users to quickly correct mistakes or accidental changes. *Hence, statement D is correct.*
 
• In many advanced software programs like **Adobe Photoshop**, **Microsoft Word**, or **Visual Studio Code**, this shortcut can be pressed repeatedly to **reverse** a sequence of multiple actions stored in the **undo history**.
 
• This feature is a fundamental part of the **Graphical User Interface (GUI)** design philosophy, encouraging **non-destructive editing** by providing a safety net for users during complex tasks.
 
• The **Ctrl+Z** command is widely supported across various **file explorers**, **text editors**, **web browsers**, and **integrated development environments (IDEs)** globally.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ctrl+U (Underline):**

 
 
• This shortcut is used to **underline** selected text in word processing applications like **MS Word** and **Google Docs**.
 
• It is a **text-formatting** feature used to emphasize specific content or **headings** within a document. *Hence, statement A is incorrect in the context of undoing actions.*
 
 
 
• **Ctrl+E (Center Alignment):**
 
 
• In software like **Microsoft PowerPoint** or **Word**, this shortcut is used to **center align** the selected paragraph or text block.
 
• In certain **web browsers** like **Chrome** or **Edge**, it may also be used to focus the **address bar** for a search query. *Hence, statement B is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Ctrl+X (Cut):**
 
 
• The **Ctrl+X** shortcut is used to **cut** a selected item, such as text, a file, or an image, and move it to the **system clipboard**.
 
• Unlike copying (Ctrl+C), "cutting" removes the item from its original **location** so it can be **pasted** (Ctrl+V) elsewhere. *Hence, statement C is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Redo Functionality:**
 
 
• The opposite of the undo function is **Redo**, which is typically mapped to the **Ctrl+Y** shortcut in **Windows** or **Cmd+Shift+Z** in **macOS**.
 
• This allows users to re-apply an action that was previously reversed by the **undo** command.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:** The "Undo" concept and its **shortcut** were popularized by **Xerox PARC** in the **1970s** and later standardized by **Apple** and **Microsoft** in the **1980s** to improve **human-computer interaction**.
 
• **Application Variety:** While **Ctrl+Z** is near-universal for "Undo," its behavior can vary; for example, in a **Command Prompt** or **Terminal**, **Ctrl+Z** might be used to **suspend** a running process rather than undo text input.
 
• **Software Limitations:** Some applications have a limited **undo buffer**, meaning they can only remember a **finite number** of actions (e.g., the last **20** to **100** actions) before the oldest actions are permanently saved and cannot be reverted.
 
• **Productivity Impact:** Mastering these **keyboard shortcuts** significantly increases **workflow efficiency** and **digital literacy** for professionals across industries, from **data entry** to **software engineering**.

questions.question: In 2025, which international organization reclassified India’s de facto exchange rate regime from a “stabilised” system to a crawl-like arrangement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**International Monetary Fund (IMF)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** is the global organization responsible for the **Article IV consultation**, which involves a periodic review of a member country's economic health and its exchange rate policies.
 
• In **2025**, following an assessment of the **Indian Rupee's (INR)** performance against the **US Dollar**, the **IMF** reclassified **India’s** de facto exchange rate regime from a **stabilised arrangement** to a **crawl-like arrangement**.
 
• A **crawl-like arrangement** is a technical classification used when the exchange rate remains within a narrow margin of **2%** relative to a statistically identified trend for a period of at least **6 months**.
 
• This reclassification indicates that the **IMF** observed the exchange rate moving in a more predictable trend compared to the earlier **stabilised** classification, where the currency was kept within a very tight range without a definitive trend.
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** often contests such reclassifications, maintaining that its interventions in the **Foreign Exchange Market** are only intended to curb **volatility** rather than to target a specific exchange rate level or trend.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **International Monetary Fund (IMF):**

 
 
• Established in **1944** during the **Bretton Woods Conference**, the **IMF** is headquartered in **Washington, D.C.**, and currently has **190 member countries**.
 
• The primary mission of the **IMF** is to ensure the stability of the **international monetary system**, facilitate **international trade**, and provide **financial assistance** to countries facing **balance of payments** crises.
 
• The organization is currently led by **Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva** (as of **2024-2025**).
 
 
 
• **Exchange Rate Classifications:**
 
 
• **Stabilised Arrangement:** Occurs when the exchange rate remains within a **2%** margin against an anchor currency for at least **6 months** but does not follow a specific trend.
 
• **Floating:** A regime where the exchange rate is largely market-determined, with interventions by the **Central Bank** being rare and aimed only at managing market conditions.
 
• **India** officially describes its regime as **floating** (de jure), but the **IMF** assigns a de facto classification based on observed market data.
 
 
 
• **Special Drawing Rights (SDR):**
 
 
• The **SDR** is an international reserve asset created by the **IMF** in **1969** to supplement its member countries' official reserves. Its value is based on a basket of five currencies: the **US Dollar**, **Euro**, **Chinese Renminbi**, **Japanese Yen**, and **British Pound Sterling**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

questions.question: According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), 2025, reporting based on 2023 data, which greenhouse gas/gases reached 151% of its/their pre-industrial concentration?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Carbon dioxide**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **World Meteorological Organization (WMO)** Greenhouse Gas Bulletin released in **October 2024** (providing data for **2023**), global average surface concentrations of **Carbon dioxide (CO2)** reached **420.0 parts per million (ppm)**.
 
• This concentration represents **151%** of the **pre-industrial** level (before the year **1750**), which was approximately **278 ppm**. Hence, the statement regarding **Carbon dioxide** reaching this specific threshold is correct.
 
• **Carbon dioxide** is the most significant long-lived greenhouse gas in the atmosphere, responsible for approximately **64%** of the total **radiative forcing** (warming effect) since **1750**.
 
• The primary drivers for the increase in **CO2** levels are the **burning of fossil fuels** (coal, oil, and gas), **cement production**, and **land-use changes** such as large-scale deforestation.
 
• The **WMO** report highlights that as long as emissions continue, **greenhouse gases** will continue to accumulate in the atmosphere, leading to rising **global temperatures**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Methane (CH4)**:

 
 
• In **2023**, atmospheric **Methane** reached **1934 parts per billion (ppb)**.
 
• This level is **265%** of the **pre-industrial** level. About **40%** of methane is emitted from natural sources (like wetlands), while **60%** comes from human activities such as **rice agriculture**, **livestock**, and **landfills**.
 
 
 
• **Nitrous Oxide (N2O)**:
 
 
• The concentration of **Nitrous Oxide** reached **336.9 ppb** in **2023**.
 
• This is **125%** of its **pre-industrial** value. It is both a potent greenhouse gas and an **ozone-depleting substance**, primarily emitted from **nitrogen fertilizers** and industrial processes.
 
 
 
• **Radiative Forcing**:
 
 
• The **Annual Greenhouse Gas Index (AGGI)** shows that from **1990** to **2023**, the warming effect from long-lived greenhouse gases increased by **51.5%**, with **CO2** contributing about **80%** of this increase.
 
 
 
• **World Meteorological Organization (WMO)**:
 
 
• The **WMO** is a specialized agency of the **United Nations (UN)** established in **1950**.
 
• It is headquartered in **Geneva, Switzerland**, and serves as the authoritative voice on the state of the Earth's atmosphere and **climate change**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Industrial Revolution** (starting around **1750**) marked the point where human activity began to significantly alter the atmospheric composition through **mechanization** and **fossil fuel** use.
 
• The **Paris Agreement** aims to limit global warming to well below **2 degrees Celsius**, preferably to **1.5 degrees Celsius**, compared to **pre-industrial** levels.
 
• **Greenhouse gas** concentrations are measured in **parts per million (ppm)** or **parts per billion (ppb)**, indicating the number of molecules of the gas per million or billion molecules of dry air.
 
• The **2024 Bulletin** underscores that the **1.5°C target** is becoming increasingly difficult to achieve due to the "clumping" of **CO2** in the atmosphere, which stays for **centuries**.

questions.question: Who among the following leaders founded the Indian National Association in 1876?

options.text: Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale
Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose

questions.solution:
